Paper_name: Judging me and you: Task design modulates self-prioritization
Summary: Probing the boundary conditions of the self-prioritization effect (SPE), this investigation explored whether basic aspects of task design modulate self-bias. In two experiments (simultaneous and sequential versions of a standard shape-label matching task), self-prioritization was reduced when stimulus presentation was blocked (i.e., self- or friend-relevant items) compared to intermixed (i.e., self- and friend-relevant items). The findings highlight both the persistence of self-prioritization and its sensitivity to task-related variation.
Author: Marius Golubickis, C. Neil Macrae
Conclusion: Across both simultaneous and sequential versions of the shape-label matching task, basic aspects of the task design moderated self-prioritization: the benefits of self-relevance were less pronounced when stimuli were blocked compared to intermixed. Although a standard SPE (self < friend < stranger) emerged on response speed in both presentation conditions, it was markedly reduced under blocked presentations. Blocked (vs. mixed) presentations also eliminated the accuracy advantage of self-related items in Experiment 1. Task design attenuated but did not abolish self-prioritization during decisional processing.
